lesson.title: Verifying a Maximum: Proving the Peak Is Really a Peak
lesson.summary: A critical point is only a candidate. Learn the two rigorous ways to confirm it is genuinely the highest point, a sign change in the first derivative or a negative second derivative, then use the Candidates Test to confirm it is the global maximum.
lesson.body:
Setting f'(x) = 0 and solving for x finds candidates, not answers. A critical point could be a maximum, a minimum, or neither, and the only way to know which is to run one of two verification tools: the First Derivative Test or the Second Derivative Test.

The First Derivative Test checks the sign of f'(x) on either side of the critical point. If f'(x) is positive just to the left (the function is rising) and negative just to the right (the function is falling), the critical point is a local maximum, the function climbed up to it and then came back down. The Second Derivative Test instead checks concavity directly at the critical point: if f''(c) < 0, the graph curves downward like the top of a hill at that point, which is exactly the shape of a local maximum.

Consider a profit function P(x) = -3x^2 + 120x - 300 for x >= 0, representing profit in dollars from producing x units of a good. Differentiate: P'(x) = -6x + 120. Setting this to zero gives x = 20.

Apply the First Derivative Test: at x = 0, just left of the critical point, P'(0) = 120, which is positive, so the function is rising there. At x = 30, just right of the critical point, P'(30) = -180 + 120 = -60, which is negative, so the function is falling there. The sign change from positive to negative confirms x = 20 is a local maximum.

Apply the Second Derivative Test as a cross check: P''(x) = -6, a constant that is negative everywhere. Since P'' never changes sign, the function is concave down across its entire domain, not just near x = 20, which means this local maximum is automatically the global maximum as well, no other critical point could possibly compete with it. The maximum profit is P(20) = -3(400) + 2400 - 300 = -1200 + 2400 - 300 = 900 dollars.

To fully confirm x = 20 is the global maximum on the whole domain x >= 0, run the Candidates Test: compare the critical point's value against the domain's boundary and its long run behavior. At the left endpoint, P(0) = -300. As x grows without bound, the -3x^2 term dominates and P(x) approaches negative infinity. Among all the candidates, the endpoint value -300, the unbounded tail heading to negative infinity, and the interior critical value 900, the critical point at x = 20 wins decisively. That combination, a verified critical point plus a domain-wide comparison, is what turns "we found a candidate" into "we proved this is the maximum."
